clue: Dome-shaped muscle that does most of the work of breathing.
why: The diaphragm separates chest from abdomen. When it contracts it flattens and pulls air into the lungs.
pearl: Hiccups are sudden spasms of the diaphragm, followed by the vocal cords snapping shut: that’s the “hic”.

clue: What you feel at the wrist, about 60 to 100 times a minute at rest.
why: The pulse is the wave of pressure from each heartbeat, felt where an artery runs close to the skin.
pearl: The radial pulse sits on the thumb side of the wrist. Use two fingers, not your thumb, which has its own pulse.

clue: Body temperature of 38°C or more.
why: A fever is a raised body temperature, usually the immune system responding to infection.
pearl: Fever is deliberate: the hypothalamus turns the body’s thermostat up on purpose.

clue: Hormone from the pancreas that lets cells take up glucose.
why: Insulin lowers blood glucose by helping muscle, fat and liver cells absorb it. Type 1 diabetes means the body can’t make it.
pearl: It was first purified and used as a treatment in Toronto in 1922, turning type 1 diabetes from a death sentence into a manageable condition.

clue: Health professional who cares for people through pregnancy and birth.
why: Midwives care for women and birthing people through pregnancy, labour, birth and the weeks after.
pearl: The word comes from Old English for “with woman”.

clue: Too little haemoglobin to carry enough oxygen.
why: Anaemia means a low haemoglobin level. Tiredness, breathlessness and pale skin are common.
pearl: Iron deficiency is the most common cause worldwide, and heavy periods are a big reason for it in women.

clue: Throbbing, often one-sided headache, sometimes with an aura.
why: Migraine is a neurological condition with recurrent headaches, often with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound.
pearl: It is about three times more common in women than in men.

clue: Iron-containing protein that makes red blood cells red.
why: Haemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that picks up oxygen in the lungs and drops it off in the tissues.
pearl: Each haemoglobin molecule can carry up to four oxygen molecules.

clue: Paired organs where oxygen goes in and carbon dioxide comes out.
why: The lungs swap gases across millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli.
pearl: The left lung is smaller than the right, to make room for the heart.

clue: Twelve pairs of curved bones that guard the chest.
why: The ribs protect the heart and lungs and move with every breath.
pearl: A small number of people have an extra rib in the neck, called a cervical rib.

clue: Trains the immune system before the real infection turns up.
why: A vaccine teaches the immune system to recognise a germ, so it can respond quickly if it meets the real thing.
pearl: The word comes from vacca, Latin for cow, after Edward Jenner’s cowpox work in the 1790s.

clue: Mouth fluid. You make roughly a litre a day.
why: Saliva moistens food, protects teeth and starts digestion.
pearl: It contains amylase, an enzyme that starts breaking down starch before you’ve even swallowed.

clue: Tendency to recurrent, unprovoked seizures.
why: Epilepsy is a brain condition with repeated seizures. There are many types and causes.
pearl: About 50 million people worldwide live with epilepsy. The WHO says up to 70% could be seizure-free with the right treatment.

clue: Condition where blood glucose runs too high.
why: Diabetes means the body can’t make enough insulin or can’t use it well, so blood glucose rises.
pearl: World Diabetes Day is 14 November, the birthday of Frederick Banting, who co-discovered insulin.

clue: Main group of female sex hormones.
why: Oestrogens are made mostly by the ovaries before menopause. They shape periods, pregnancy, bones and more.
pearl: Men make it too: an enzyme called aromatase converts some testosterone into oestrogen.

clue: The largest health profession in the world.
why: Nurses assess, treat, educate and care for patients across every part of health care.
pearl: Nurses make up more than half of the world’s health professionals, according to the WHO.

clue: Open sore on the skin or a lining, like the stomach’s.
why: An ulcer is a break in the skin or a lining that is slow to heal.
pearl: Most stomach ulcers are caused by H. pylori bacteria or anti-inflammatory medicines. Marshall and Warren won the 2005 Nobel Prize for the bacteria link.

clue: Light-sensing layer at the back of the eye.
why: The retina turns light into nerve signals that travel to the brain along the optic nerve.
pearl: The image lands on it upside down. Your brain quietly flips it.

clue: Life-threatening body-wide reaction to infection.
why: Sepsis happens when the body’s response to infection starts damaging its own organs. It is a medical emergency.
pearl: It was linked to about 11 million deaths worldwide in 2017, around one in five of all deaths.

clue: Ringing or buzzing in the ears with no outside sound.
why: Tinnitus is hearing a sound, like ringing, hissing or buzzing, that has no outside source.
pearl: The word comes from the Latin tinnire, “to ring”.

clue: Immune skin condition with thick red plaques and silvery scale.
why: Psoriasis is a long-term immune condition that speeds up skin cell turnover, causing scaly plaques.
pearl: It isn’t contagious. Up to 3 in 10 people with it also develop psoriatic arthritis.

clue: Health professional who tests hearing.
why: Audiologists assess hearing and balance and fit hearing aids and other devices.
pearl: Many Deaf people see deafness as a culture and a language identity, not something to fix. Capital-D Deaf refers to that community.

clue: Dried crust over a healing graze.
why: A scab is dried blood and fibrin that protects a wound while new skin grows underneath.
pearl: Picking it off slows healing and makes a scar more likely.

clue: The largest joint in the body.
why: The knee joins the thigh bone to the shin bone, with the kneecap in front.
pearl: The kneecap is the body’s largest sesamoid bone: a bone that grows inside a tendon.

clue: Tissue like the uterine lining growing outside the uterus.
why: Endometriosis causes tissue similar to the lining of the uterus to grow elsewhere, often causing pain and sometimes infertility.
pearl: It affects around 1 in 10 women and girls of reproductive age worldwide, and diagnosis often takes years.

clue: Airways narrow and wheeze, often triggered by pollen or cold air.
why: Asthma is a long-term condition where the airways become inflamed and narrow, causing wheeze, cough and breathlessness.
pearl: Australia has one of the highest asthma rates in the world: about 1 in 9 people.

clue: Stress hormone from the adrenal glands, highest in the morning.
why: Cortisol helps control blood glucose, blood pressure and the stress response.
pearl: Levels normally peak soon after waking and fall to their lowest around midnight.

clue: Organ behind the stomach that makes enzymes and insulin.
why: The pancreas makes digestive enzymes and hormones, including insulin and glucagon.
pearl: Its hormone-making cells sit in clusters called the islets of Langerhans.

clue: Doctor’s listening tube.
why: A stethoscope carries sounds from the heart, lungs and bowel to the listener’s ears.
pearl: René Laennec invented it in 1816, reportedly to avoid putting his ear on a patient’s chest.

clue: Thigh bone, the longest in the body.
why: The femur runs from the hip to the knee and carries the body’s weight.
pearl: It is roughly a quarter of your height.
